title: DNA Solves 250-Year Mystery of Vanished Crocodiles!
summary: Did you know that crocodiles can surf? Well, not exactly, but they are amazing ocean travelers! Scientists just solved a 250-year-old mystery about crocodiles that used to live on the Seychelles, a group of islands in the Indian Ocean. Early explorers wrote about seeing crocodiles there, but after people settled on the islands in 1770, the crocodiles were gone within 50 years. No one knew exactly what kind of crocodiles they were—until now. Researchers from Germany and the Seychelles studied DNA from old crocodile bones in museums. They compared it to DNA from saltwater crocodiles alive today. The result? The Seychelles crocodiles were saltwater crocodiles (Crocodylus porosus)! These are the biggest reptiles in the world—males can grow over 6 meters long, about the length of a small school bus. Saltwater crocodiles have special glands that let them get rid of extra salt, so they can live in the ocean for a long time. The scientists think the first crocodiles to reach the Seychelles drifted at least 3,000 kilometers across the Indian Ocean, maybe even farther. That's like floating from New York to Los Angeles! They probably rode ocean currents over many generations. Today, saltwater crocodiles live in many places, from India to Australia. But before the Seychelles population was wiped out, their range stretched over 12,000 kilometers—from Vanuatu in the Pacific all the way to the Seychelles. This discovery shows how connected animal populations can be, even across huge oceans. It also reminds us how quickly humans can change an ecosystem. Next time you see a crocodile, remember: they're not just swamp creatures—they're long-distance ocean voyagers!
why_it_matters: This discovery shows that even tough creatures like crocodiles can disappear because of humans, and it teaches us to protect animals so they don't vanish from more places.

background_read: The Seychelles are a beautiful group of islands in the Indian Ocean, famous for giant tortoises and rare birds. Early explorers like French settlers wrote about seeing crocodiles basking on the beaches.
Saltwater crocodiles (the world's largest living reptile, up to 6 meters long) are incredible ocean travelers. They can float and drift using ocean currents, sometimes crossing huge distances.
Scientists used DNA from museum bones, comparing ancient crocodile genes to those of modern saltwater crocodiles. DNA works like a family tree book, showing which animals are closely related.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers from Germany and the Seychelles
WHAT: Solved a 250-year-old mystery—the crocodiles that once lived on the Seychelles were saltwater crocodiles
WHERE: The Seychelles islands in the Indian Ocean
WHY: To understand how these giant reptiles crossed oceans and to see how quickly humans can wipe out a local animal population

perspectives.description: They see this as a sad reminder that human settlement can wipe out a species very fast, and we must be careful with island ecosystems today.
They are excited because ancient DNA can crack historical puzzles, showing how connected animal populations were across oceans.
Some might say it doesn't change much because saltwater crocodiles still live elsewhere, but locally it's a big loss of biodiversity.
